vignette:
He sits at his desk in the precinct, the fluorescent lights humming overhead. The case file in front of him is open to a photograph of a woman’s bruised forearm, and he feels his own arm begin to ache. He does not look away. He has learned that looking away only makes it worse later, when the image comes back unbidden. He is thirty-four months into his marriage to Sarah, and still, sometimes, when she reaches for his hand in the dark, his body flinches before his mind can stop it.

Four years ago, he was living with a woman named Corinne. She was a prosecutor, sharp and funny, and he loved the way she could deconstruct an argument over dinner. The first time she hit him, it was after a case had gone badly. He had said the wrong thing—something about needing space. Her open palm connected with his cheek, and he stood there, stunned, more confused than hurt. He told himself it was a one-time thing, a release valve for pressure she carried. He was a detective; he knew the statistics. He also knew he loved her.

The second time was a closed fist, aimed at his ribs while he slept. He woke up gasping and she was already apologizing, tears streaming down her face, promising it would never happen again. He stayed. He stayed through the black eye he lied about at work—a fall during a chase, he said. He stayed through the night she locked him out of their apartment in January, and he stood in the hallway in his socks, phone dead, knowing everyone in the building could hear her screaming. He did not call the police. He was the police. He knew how those calls ended: with the male suspect in cuffs, regardless of who threw the first punch.

The relationship ended when he finally arrested her—not for assaulting him, but for violating a protection order he had never filed. A neighbor had called it in, and he was the responding officer. He remembers the look on her face when she saw him in the doorway, the way she laughed and said, “You think this makes you the good guy?” He put her in the back of the squad car and then sat in the driver’s seat for twenty minutes, shaking, before he could turn the key.

Now, he is a detective in the same precinct, and domestic violence calls are his specialty. He volunteers for them. His lieutenant thinks it is dedication. In truth, it is a kind of exposure therapy he never asked for, and it is not working. When he interviews victims, he feels a swell of rage that he masks with professional calm. When suspects lie, he sees Corinne’s eyes. When he goes home, he sometimes checks the locks three times, then checks them again. Sarah has stopped asking why.

His PCL-5 score, administered by the department psychologist after a particularly bad night shift, sits at 72. He knows what that means. Severe. He has not told Sarah the number. He has not told her about the nightmares where he is back in that hallway, barefoot, pounding on a door that will not open. He has not told her that he keeps a go bag in the trunk of his car, with a change of clothes and cash, just in case. He does not know if he is waiting to run or waiting to be hurt again.

He closes the case file and rubs his arm. Sarah is making pasta for dinner. She will ask about his day, and he will tell her about the paperwork, not about the photographs. She will kiss his forehead, and for a moment, he will feel safe. Then he will lie awake, listening to the house settle, his heart thudding against his ribs like a fist against a locked door.
